meta_description: The HOA insurance appraisal process explained step by step for Texas boards: invoking appraisal, evidence, timelines and deductibles. Get a free review.
h1: HOA Insurance Appraisal Process: A Step-by-Step Guide for Texas Boards
excerpt: How Texas HOA and condo boards use the appraisal clause to resolve master policy disputes: each step, board duties, evidence, timelines and deductible issues.
key_takeaways: HOA appraisal resolves disputes over the amount of loss, not coverage.
Boards should confirm authority under governing documents before invoking appraisal.
Organize evidence building by building to speed up the panel review.
Texas percentage wind and hail deductibles can change the net recovery significantly.
An award signed by two of three panel members sets the amount of loss.
body_html:
The HOA insurance appraisal process lets a homeowners or condominium association resolve a dispute with its carrier over the amount of a covered loss. The board invokes the policy's appraisal clause, each side names an independent appraiser, the appraisers inspect and price the damage, and an umpire breaks any deadlock. Two signatures make the award binding.

What is the HOA insurance appraisal process?

Most association master policies, like most Texas property policies, contain an appraisal clause. It gives either the association or the insurer the right to demand appraisal when the two sides agree a loss happened but cannot agree on what it is worth.

For an HOA, that disagreement is rarely small. A single hailstorm can damage dozens of roofs, gutters, fences, clubhouse finishes and pool equipment across an entire community. When the carrier's estimate covers only part of that damage, appraisal offers a faster, less expensive path than a lawsuit to a figure both sides must honor.

Appraisal is not mediation and it is not a trial. It is a contractual process focused on one question: the amount of loss. If you want the fundamentals first, read what an insurance appraisal is.

Why HOA claims end up in appraisal

Association claims are larger and more complex than single-family claims, which creates more room for disagreement. The most common friction points include:

  • Scope across many buildings. The carrier approves roofs on some buildings and denies others that took the same storm.
  • Repair versus replacement. The adjuster calls for spot repairs while the association's roofer says the system needs replacement.
  • Matching and uniformity. Patching a few elevations with mismatched siding or shingles can leave a community looking inconsistent.
  • Pricing. Unit costs that do not reflect what contractors actually charge for large, multi-building projects.
  • Common elements. Fences, mailbox kiosks, gates, amenity buildings and landscaping features left off the estimate.
  • Deductibles. Percentage wind and hail deductibles that apply per building or per occurrence, which changes the net recovery.

Many of these issues mirror what we see in multi-family insurance claim disputes and apartment complex appraisals, though HOAs add a governance layer that apartment owners do not have.

Step-by-step: how HOA appraisal works

Every policy's clause is worded a little differently, so always read your association's master policy. The typical sequence looks like this:

StepWhat happensWho handles it
1. Policy and authority reviewConfirm the appraisal clause wording and that the board has authority to actBoard, manager, association counsel
2. Written demandThe association sends a written appraisal demand identifying the claim and the disputed amountBoard or its representative
3. Appraiser selectionEach side names a competent, disinterested appraiser, often within about 20 days of the demandAssociation and carrier
4. Umpire selectionThe two appraisers agree on an umpire, or either side asks a court to appoint oneAppraisers
5. Inspection and estimatingAppraisers inspect each building and common element and prepare line-item estimatesAppraisers
6. NegotiationAppraisers compare scope and pricing and try to agree line by lineAppraisers
7. Umpire reviewIf disagreements remain, the umpire reviews the evidence and decides disputed itemsUmpire
8. AwardA written award signed by any two of the three becomes the amount of lossTwo of three panel members

After the award, the carrier applies deductibles, prior payments, depreciation and policy limits, then issues payment. Holdback amounts for replacement cost are typically released once repairs are completed.

Board responsibilities during HOA appraisal

An HOA board acts on behalf of every owner, so it needs to handle appraisal carefully and transparently.

Confirm authority and document decisions

Check the declaration, bylaws and any management agreement to confirm who can invoke appraisal and sign related documents. Record the decision in board minutes. If you have questions about authority under your governing documents or the Texas Property Code, talk to the association's attorney. This article is general information, not legal advice.

Clarify what the master policy covers

In many communities, the master policy covers common elements and building exteriors while unit owners carry their own HO-6 or HO-3 policies for interiors and personal property. In others, the association insures the full structures. Knowing that split prevents the association from appraising items it does not insure, or missing items it does.

Communicate with owners

Owners want to know when roofs will be fixed. Give regular, factual updates on the process without sharing negotiating positions. A short timeline in the community newsletter goes a long way.

Evidence that strengthens an HOA appraisal

Appraisal panels decide based on evidence. Associations that organize documentation early tend to have smoother appraisals. Useful items include:

  • A building-by-building inventory with addresses or building numbers, roof areas and materials
  • Date-stamped photos and drone imagery of each roof slope and elevation
  • Prior maintenance and inspection reports showing pre-storm condition
  • Weather data for the date of loss, such as hail reports from the National Weather Service
  • Contractor bids and line-item Xactimate or Symbility estimates
  • Owner reports of leaks and interior damage, logged by unit and date
  • 3D scans of amenity buildings or interior common areas

For large communities, Matterport 3D documentation creates a permanent, measurable record of clubhouses and interior common areas before repairs begin. Our free claim documentation checklist is a good starting point for managers organizing files.

Tip: Organize every photo, report and bid by building number. Appraisers and umpires move much faster when they can review one building at a time instead of searching through an unsorted folder.

HOA appraisal in Texas: storms, deductibles and timing

Texas associations face some of the most active severe weather in the country. North Texas communities in Dallas, Frisco, McKinney and Plano see repeated spring hail. Central Texas towns from Round Rock to Georgetown face hail and wind. Coastal communities near Houston and Galveston contend with hurricanes and tropical storms.

Three Texas-specific points come up often in HOA claims:

  1. Percentage deductibles. Many Texas policies carry wind and hail deductibles stated as a percentage of insured value. Whether that applies per building or per occurrence can swing the net recovery significantly.
  2. Prompt payment rules. Texas Insurance Code chapter 542 sets deadlines for carriers to acknowledge, decide and pay claims. Appraisal does not erase those rules, and the Texas Supreme Court addressed their interaction in Barbara Technologies v. State Farm Lloyds (2019).
  3. Pre-suit notice. For weather claims, chapter 542A generally requires 61 days' written notice before a lawsuit. Associations considering litigation alongside appraisal should be aware of that timeline.

Our Dallas insurance appraiser page covers North Texas storm patterns in more detail.

How long does HOA appraisal take?

A single-building residential appraisal can wrap up in a couple of months. HOA appraisals usually take longer because of the number of structures, the size of the estimates and the scheduling involved. A community of a few dozen buildings might take several months from demand to award, depending on how quickly appraisers are named, how accessible the property is and whether an umpire is needed.

Within that window, the HOA appraisal itself usually moves in phases: building inspections first, then estimate exchange, then negotiation and, if needed, umpire review. Boards can ask their appraiser for a realistic schedule at the start so owners know what to expect.

The biggest delays come from slow appraiser selection, disputes over umpire appointment and incomplete documentation. Boards that respond quickly and keep records organized shorten the timeline. Roof-heavy claims often benefit from reviewing commercial roof hail damage claim issues in advance, since many HOA buildings use similar systems.

Common mistakes in the HOA insurance appraisal process

Most problems in the HOA insurance appraisal process are avoidable. These are the mistakes we see boards make most often:

  • Waiting too long. Months pass while the board debates, roofs keep leaking, and interior damage grows. Delay also makes it harder to separate storm damage from later deterioration.
  • Appraising only part of the loss. A demand that lists only roofs can leave fences, gutters, amenity buildings and interior common areas out of the award.
  • Naming a partial appraiser. Most clauses require a disinterested appraiser. Choosing someone with a financial stake in the repair contract invites a challenge to the award.
  • Relying on a single summary bid. A lump-sum roofing proposal is hard for a panel to compare. Line-item estimates that match the carrier's format are far more persuasive.
  • Ignoring deductible structure. If the policy applies a percentage deductible per building, the board needs to understand which buildings actually clear the deductible before it sets expectations with owners.
  • Poor recordkeeping. Missing minutes, unclear authority and scattered files slow everything down and can create disputes later.

A short planning meeting with your manager, counsel and appraiser before the demand goes out can prevent nearly all of these problems.

Choosing an appraiser for your association

The association's appraiser should be competent, independent and experienced with multi-building claims. Look for someone who:

  • Has written and defended large line-item estimates in Xactimate or Symbility
  • Understands roofing systems, matching issues and common-element construction
  • Can explain findings clearly to a board that may not have construction experience
  • Is familiar with how umpires evaluate evidence; see what an insurance umpire does

Joseph Dittman, the appraiser behind TX Insurance Appraiser, has spent his career on the policyholder side of Texas property claims, inspecting hail, wind, water and fire losses and building detailed estimates that hold up to scrutiny.

Next steps for HOA boards

If your association's claim has stalled over scope or price, start by gathering the master policy, the carrier's estimate, your contractor bids and a building-by-building damage summary. Compare them side by side so the board understands exactly where the gap is.

faqs.q: Who can invoke appraisal for a homeowners association?
faqs.a: Usually the board, acting for the association as the named insured on the master policy. Governing documents may set who can sign and how decisions are approved. Many boards record the vote in meeting minutes and consult association counsel before sending a written appraisal demand to the carrier.

faqs.q: Can individual unit owners use the HOA master policy appraisal clause?
faqs.a: Generally no. The appraisal clause belongs to the named insured, which is typically the association. Unit owners with damage to interiors or personal property may have appraisal rights under their own HO-6 or HO-3 policies, depending on how responsibility is split in the governing documents and policy forms.

faqs.q: Does HOA appraisal cover every building in the community?
faqs.a: It covers whatever disputed items the demand and the claim include. Associations often appraise all damaged buildings and common elements together under one claim, with estimates broken out building by building. That structure helps the panel apply per-building deductibles and limits correctly afterward.

faqs.q: Who pays for the appraisers in an HOA appraisal?
faqs.a: Under most appraisal clauses, each side pays its own appraiser, and the umpire fee is split equally between the association and the insurer. Check the master policy for the exact language. Appraiser fee structures vary, so boards should get the fee agreement in writing before the process starts.

faqs.q: What happens after the HOA appraisal award is signed?
faqs.a: The carrier applies the deductible, prior payments, depreciation and limits to the award amount and issues payment, typically within the time allowed under its policy and Texas law. Replacement cost holdbacks are usually released after repairs are completed and documented.
